We evaluated Gemini 4 Argon in 100 unsaturated, competitive and cooperative coding environments. It's roughly in between Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 in our testing, so it's maybe 2 months behind the frontier. Google's major releases have usually done pretty well on our benchmarks because they're good at hard problems and open-ended decision making (with a well specified prompt), which obviously doesn't always translate to user experience. In particular, older Google models struggled to work efficiently in a harness. They seem to have solved that with Argon. We did see a new problem which I hope they can fix. This is the first near-frontier model we've caught in infinite reasoning loops in a long time. We also saw a few examples of it failing to properly delineate reasoning blocks, so it has a higher failure rate than its competitors. My overall impression is that Argon is a near-frontier model for engineering design, code analysis, and chat. It definitely has the intelligence to be a competitive coding assistant product, but a good coding assistant needs to be polished, so I hope they can clean up the CoT bugs. Data at http

No one is actually one-shotting new code on top of the existing repo and just checking it in. Even in a simplistic case, it’s multiturn. You give it a prompt, and it writes some code, tries to build it, and it doesn’t work. So then it keeps iterating, and changes some more code until it builds and then does the same thing again until it passes tests. And if you have a complex system, it might do a lot more CI. The input to this is not just the preexisting code, the prompt you provide, and some random seeds. It’s also the output from every single tool invoked, which means you need to record the state of every single tool and every file that was read, every API that was called. It means that you can’t upgrade Claude. It means that you can’t upgrade the compiler. If you change anything in the state of the world you no longer have replicability. Aside from all that, I don’t know why you would want this anyway. Storing a bunch of prompts doesn’t seem to actually gain anything even if it worked.

Ok, I guess I have karma to burn for the inevitable downvotes.. "I've" been writing a compiler. It's pretty good - comparable to C++/gcc/clang in speed and has some (IMHO) nice features, amongst which: - it doesn't use header files, for library imports it reads the DWARF to get method/funciton signatures and types - it has the nicest interface I've ever seen for a GPU/CPU interconnect, just one line of code identifies the bit to convert to a GPU kernel, and I'm working on getting rid of that too. - the same language is used for the GPU and CPU, so the below is a full and complete GPU-driven Mandelbrot program. On my M4 Max MBP it operates in 0.7ms on the GPU, 94ms on all-cores (another option it can do) or 432ms on a single core. #use "Stdio.xc" #use "Par.xc" #define W 2048 i32 main(void) { u32 total = 0; par mandel :reduce(+ total) { for (u32 i in 0..W * W) { float cx = (float)(i % W) * (3.0f / W) - 2.0f; float cy = (float)(i / W) * (3.0f / W) - 1.5f; float x = 0.0f; float y = 0.0f; u32 k = 0; while (k < 256 && x * x + y * y < 4.0f) { float xt = x * x - y * y + cx; y = 2.0f * x * y + cy; x = xt; k = k + 1; } total = total + k; } } printf("%u iterations\n", total); return 0; } - The 'par' line is the only thing that is a bit different from a 'C'-like language, all the data-hazards between CPU/GPU are taken care of, and there's no setup boilerplate. xc will compile the above straight out of the box. - Currently working on automatic division of labour between any GPUs on the same machine, initial results are promising, and then onwards to GPUs on the LAN. - Binding of the GPU happens at runtime, not compile-time, meaning the best possible execution path will be chosen (by measuring, then persisting the measurement so it doesn't have to run again for the same parameters) on any given machine, be that an NVIDIA, AMD, or Apple platform, or a WGSL-based browser. Anyway. Brief synopsis over with. The point is that a lot of the above things are my own ideas, there isn't really anything out there (that I know of) that parses DWARF for data. There's no language out there (that I know of) that has such a clean interface between CPU and GPU, Runtime measurement and efficiency management built in, with persistence, complete independence from vendor tools. Etc. etc. This isn't just a "hey Claude, build me a compiler, I want it to be rad, yo" minimal-effort thing - I've spent more than half a year doing this, there's been a lot of effort involved, steering, redirecting when things don't pan out, discussing, overrriding the recommended path in the name of future goals, etc. Don't get me wrong, I've written compilers before, literal decades ago (I'm retired now), so I know just what a huge job it was to take on, and I'd never have attempted it myself if the LLM wasn't there to do the grunt work, but there's still a lot of "me" in this. My vision. My direction. My time. What I have previously done is say "I" wrote the compiler (though that's been too subtle in the past) so I now tend to say "I wrote a compiler (full disclosure: with Claude)". And then I ignore the people who get upset about the LLM thing, you know, like water off a duck's back.

Author here. I’ve been running this experiment for a couple of years whenever a new model comes out, and this is the first time the results have been good enough to share. I provide an LLM with a natural language specification (e.g., "an HTTP server on port 8125"), and a bash loop executes what the model generates; the actual error encountered is then fed back to the model until the test passes. There are three levels: C with gcc, assembly with as + ld, and raw bytes (where the model writes the ELF file directly, with nothing between it and the binary other than `xxd -r`). The raw bytes level isn't always reliable: in 5 runs using Claude Sonnet 5.5 on x86-64, "Hello, World" succeeded in 4 out of 5 attempts, and the HTTP server in 2 out of 5. The C and assembly levels succeeded in all 5 attempts. The system also executes binaries generated by the model, so please check what the code does before running it. I’d be happy to answer any questions

This is one of the biggest benefits. I'm not a plugin user so I don't remember how they're different from skills. Not speaking about the tool in OP specifically but regarding skills in general: you can have essentially the entire task or some of its subtasks (which you'd ordinarily direct to the agent using the skill, the main benefits of which are clearer natural language directions) handled with assistive tools written in any language your environment supports. You can additionally supply the skill with its own config files, data files, etc., building essentially a small repo within particular skills and making these resources however closely tied to the skill as you prefer. This is particularly useful when the agent would otherwise be doing a task that is programmable, or the agent is inconsistent or unable to do it in an efficient, performant or other preferred manner. The programmatic tool assistance means at least some parts of the task (possibly its entirety) could be handled in a well-tested and deterministic manner. How reliable the determinism, optimality, etc. are depends on how well you or the agent writes and verifies the code, tests, spec, etc. in the first place of course, but that only needs to be done correctly once. The other great benefit is reduced token use, potentially a massive reduction. Imagine a task Claude takes 10 minutes to prepare to do because it's reading and analyzing files for the 3rd time in the last 4 minutes, then it's asking for permissions several times in between to do this and that even after you put it in auto mode, then it's "thinking" again for the thousandth time about how to approach the task even though you had it repeat the task a hundred times already...by the time it actually starts doing the task, the most recent models are likely to have churned through tens of thousands of tokens (and that's a conservative estimate for frontier models) in the first 10 minutes. But, with tool assistance, you can have Claude directly handle some parts of that same task which, for example, needs unpredictable analysis or decision-making each time, but also have it use a set of highly optimized programs to handle the bottleneck parts or the parts you want done "your way." You could potentially cut down those 10 minutes of prep time + whatever minutes to actually do the task down to seconds, with barely a couple of thousand tokens used up! Just an example of course, but I've benefited from this strategy repeatedly across various tasks, simple ones and very complex ones. Another great thing is that the tools don't have to be tied to the skill at all, they can live anywhere in your codebase. You could even manually run the scripts like any other to handle certain tasks in their entirety or do the prep work before setting an agent loose on the remainder. There are many different approaches with different advantages. It's like actually using the agent as your...well, agent! But now you're supplying him with the latest gadgets like M/Q does for 007.

What’s even more disappointing is that I noticed a significant decline in my experience after purchasing a monthly subscription. I paid for the service expecting a better, more reliable experience, but instead, I’ve been dealing with repeated problems that make it difficult to enjoy using the app. The memory system is one of my biggest complaints. I use this app for long-running creative writing projects that involve detailed character histories, personalities, relationships, ages, and plot continuity. I can spend hours establishing these details, only for the AI to forget them, contradict them, or ignore my corrections. I repeatedly have to explain the same information because it fails to retain or consistently apply what I’ve already established. The instruction-following is just as frustrating. In a recent conversation, I explained a simple character detail, clarified my intentions several times, and explicitly stated what I wanted preserved. The AI repeatedly removed that detail anyway and kept giving me the same unwanted explanation instead of understanding my request and continuing the story. I was not asking for explicit content. I was establishing a character fact, yet the AI repeatedly treated it as something else. I’ve also experienced contradictory responses that appear inconsistent with the AI’s own previous output. I have screenshots documenting these issues. Having to argue with the software over straightforward instructions is exhausting and wastes the time I’m paying for. I understand that AI can make mistakes, but repeatedly ignoring corrections, losing context, and contradicting established information is more than a minor inconvenience. Long-term memory and instruction-following are essential for ongoing projects. If I have to maintain every detail myself and constantly correct the AI, the software is not doing its job effectively. I genuinely enjoy parts of this app, which is why these problems are so disappointing. However, noticing this decline after purchasing a monthly subscription makes the experience particularly frustrating. I want the developers to investigate the reliability issues users experience after subscribing and improve memory, context retention, consistency, and instruction-following. He did certain things, like went to a certain college, got married and had kids at particular ages, went to a certain type of grad school, took and quit certain jobs at certain times. I went through and asked, of each observation, the Bayesian question of whether the probability of that observation differed in the worlds where the hypothesis was true and false. In all 12 of my cases, where I was doing it by hand in an Excel spreadsheet using Bayes' Theorem in its probability form, I judged the observation was more likely in the world where he was indeed avoiding the Vietnam draft. I started over with Gemini with the prompt "can you evaluate the final odds for a hypothesis, given a number of observations that could be evidence for or against that hypothesis". It first laid out Bayes' Theorem in its odds form, and then asked me to lay out the hypothesis and set of observations. I did so, with it leading me through asking for three or four observations at a time. Gemini came up with its own assessment of the odds for each one, justifying the odds it gave based on historical background context like draft rules around going to college; worked up the running odds as it went; and provided a narrative interpretation. Gemini's final tally of observations was 10 in favor, 2 neutral, and 2 against, where my own by-hand analysis in a spreadsheet had come out 12-0 in favor (Gemini came up with a couple more things like inquiring about his 1969 draft lottery number). The individual odds we came up with independently were largely quite comparable. Gemini's final aggregated odds were 124,000-to-1 in favor where my spreadsheet analysis had 4600-to-1. Its final narrative assessment was that the history I described appeared to be a classic case of "draft hedge."

Hey folks; I’m the author of RemainderBot. Given your goals and task lists, it writes PRs that complete those tasks for you using excess Claude & Codex subscription tokens. As the founder of Bakeoff, I spend my time on customer development and engineering architecture & review. RemainderBot solves two problems for me and I suspect for many others out there: * There are many small tasks that require a few minutes of my time and need my context, but I just don’t have the mental energy to prioritize them, do a context shift, perform a small amount of work, and finalize the results a dozen times a day. * Some weeks I don’t get close to my Claude and Codex subscription limits. That’s a waste of what are very valuable Astra and Opus 5.5 tokens :)! RemainderBot has consistently used my goals and task lists to identify non-obvious tasks that would move me forward. It has accomplished quite a bit - 111 PRs including customer call prep, a census of 31 GitHub orgs’ agent setup files, and standalone prototypes to demo to engineers I meet with. You interact with it in whatever interface you use with GitHub PRs. It uses your comments and decisions on whether to merge PRs to guide which kinds of tasks and approaches it takes in the future. RemainderBot runs either as a manual process on your machine or as a cronjob on a server. In tick (cronjob) mode, it checks how much subscription quota is left and how much time there is until the weekly reset before picking a task and creating a PR. Here’s how you get started: * Check that git, claude (or codex), and gh CLIs exist and are authenticated on your machine * Clone the openremainderbot repo: git clone http remainderbot cd remainderbot cp -n GOALS.example.md GOALS.md cp -n sources.example.toml sources.toml Edit those two files with your personal goals and with sources for your task lists, respectively. Finally: python3 -m remainderbot snapshot python3 -m remainderbot run --provider claude --deadline-minutes 20 --size small These commands will pick a task, work on it in a new branch, and will cost you a few percent of your weekly quota. Please drop a comment on what it did for you and if it got anything wrong here or in http :). More details in the blog post - http Hope you enjoy it!

On Android, the public APIs available for digital assistants are more limited than the ones that Google gets to use for their own products. So if you want a digital assistant and you'd like to be able to hold a button on your phone and have it open a thread with an LLM (even if your screen is off), your digital assistant has to be Gemini. You can configure ChatGPT or Claude in its place, but then they can't manipulate or interact with apps in your phone very much. Or you can use an app like that for all of your LLM use but you can't conveniently summon it. Similarly, you can run local LLMs on your Google Pixel smartphone, but if you want them to be hardware accelerated using the chip that's included for that very purpose on your phone... it has to be Google's models via Google's apps. So you can't say "alright, a fast, local model which sounds great, but I want one that is trained to always run a search before answering, in a harness with good search tools for answering the kinds of practical questions I often ask", you're actually not free to put that together in a practicable way. Oh yes. Start of this year... I had an M1 MBP that I needed to re-pave with Monterey. Yes, it's end-of-support, but it's also only 4 years old. And runs on that Mac. So, first step, I make a USB installer, and run it. Great. Reboots, and says "FYI, this is an unsupported OS. You can install a newer OS instead, or run Monterey in "Reduced Security" mode." That was fine for me. "Installation of Reduced Security mode failed." Nothing else. Eventually my understanding of this was because the machine had been upgraded previously all the way to Tahoe, that somewhere along the line some firmware or something in the EFI had been upgraded and was too new for Monterey. No thanks to Apple. No info, debug logs, anything, just "Installation failed. Reboot?" So what then? Hmm, more research. "Do an IPSW image restore via DFU", i.e. pave it with a largely installed image. Could work, might have the same issue, but since I'm stuck right now, with a Mac I can't install anything on, a four year old $3,000 brick, why not? Alright, I have a Mac Studio. I get the IPSW image, and Apple Configurator. Connect the two as per Apple's instructions and the MBP does indeed show up in Configurator as being "not booted, DFU mode". Apple's instructions, "Drag the IPSW image onto the DFU 'box' for the target Mac". No. It doesn't light up like it's accepting a drag and drop, and indeed it doesn't. Nor does it accept a "restore..." or similar from the Configurator menu options. There's nothing in Configurator that seems to allow you to image the MBP. Again: no error, no instructions, just the error "bonk" noise. So... off to ChatGPT, Reddit, etc., I go. Much repeating of the same. However, ChatGPT pokes a little button. Near the very end of its answer, it says "Newer versions of macOS may have limitations on the age of the image they might restore. You may need a slightly older macOS to do this. Even an Intel MBP running Ventura could work." As fortune has it, my fiance happens to still have her old i5 MBP with touchbar, and the latest version of Ventura... let's plug it in, let it catch a little charge and boot... Alright, I need Configurator on this laptop. No soup for you, says the App Store, "You need macOS Sequoia to install Configurator". Back off to Reddit, where I find someone who has helpfully zipped up an older version of Configurator that runs on Ventura, and in the end, I'm able to re-pave via IPSW. But Apple's docs absolutely are incorrect/incomplete about Configurator, and DFU restores. "You can use Restore... in the Configurator menu to select the software image". No, you can't, even leaving aside the "old/unsupported". It actually means restoring from a "backup" (presumably Time Machine, though it doesn't specify) and you can't select any file or image. "Drag the image onto DFU". Doesn't work in that situation, no error, no "hey, you're doing the right thing but I can't do this", just acting like a fool trying to drag the image onto DFU only to have it bounce off. Like I said, I didn't have DFU port issues, but Apple's docs on how to make this happen were either non-existent, or incorrect about the process, or flat out told me I couldn't do it. But mostly non-existent and overly simplistic covering the most basic scenarios only - which I get for general support, but by the time you are "connect to a second mac in DFU mode and run Configurator" in their own words, we're way beyond simplistic "you can just install a newer macOS" type "instructions".
